name: Iron

lead: Iron is needed for oxygen transport and many enzymes. People with diffuse hair shedding, fatigue or pallor take it hoping to bring hair back to normal density, and some take it for under-eye shadows.

Follicle cells divide quickly and depend on iron-containing enzymes, and low stores are thought to push follicles early into the resting phase, causing telogen effluvium. Clinicians commonly check ferritin and haemoglobin in unexplained shedding, and correcting a confirmed deficiency is the accepted treatment for deficiency-related shedding. No randomised trial in the available research tests iron for hair outcomes.

paras: Oral iron is usually taken as a daily tablet after a blood test such as ferritin confirms low stores, often with vitamin C and apart from calcium. Shedding recovers over months as stores refill.

Oral iron commonly causes constipation, nausea and dark stools. Excess iron accumulates in people with haemochromatosis and promotes oxidative damage, and accidental overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under six. Guidance advises testing first.

social.title: New iron nanomaterial wipes out cancer cells without harming healthy tissue

angle.text: Iron is supplemented by people with diffuse hair shedding or pale skin who have low iron. Follicles depend on iron-containing enzymes, so restoring low stores lets hair cycle normally and reduces shedding. Benefits with normal iron levels are untested.

lead: Iron is an essential mineral (chemical symbol Fe) needed for oxygen transport in haemoglobin and myoglobin, for energy production, for DNA synthesis and for many enzymes [1]. About 65 to 70 percent of the roughly 3 to 4 grams of iron in the human body is bound in haemoglobin [1]. In nutrition and appearance discussions the word refers to dietary iron and oral or intravenous iron supplements rather than the metal itself, which is the subject of the general encyclopedia article [2]. Its appearance relevance is mostly through hair, skin tone, energy for training and recovery: ferritin and haemoglobin are the markers clinicians check when someone reports diffuse shedding, pallor or fatigue [3][4].

Iron deficiency, with or without anaemia, is described as the most prevalent nutritional deficiency worldwide and is especially common in women who menstruate, children, adolescents and pregnant women [5][1][6]. In looksmaxxing and physique circles iron comes up in connection with diffuse hair shedding, fatigue, pale skin and endurance in training. Clinicians commonly check ferritin and haemoglobin in people with unexplained shedding, and correcting a confirmed deficiency is the standard treatment for deficiency-related symptoms [3][4]. No randomised trial of iron supplementation for hair outcomes in people with normal iron stores was found.

Iron can also cause harm. Oral iron commonly causes gastrointestinal effects, excess iron accumulates in people with haemochromatosis and promotes oxidative damage, and accidental overdose of iron-containing products is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under six, according to product labelling [1][7].

paras: Iron is given orally or intravenously to prevent and treat iron deficiency and iron-deficiency anaemia, including in pregnancy; a US prescription iron-folic acid product, for example, is labelled for iron-deficiency and folate-deficiency anaemia and for prevention and treatment of iron deficiency in pregnancy [7]. A 2025 JAMA review addresses diagnosis and treatment of iron deficiency in adults [8]. Intravenous iron is used when oral therapy is not tolerated or ineffective and in some chronic conditions; a 2025 meta-analysis of six trials (7,175 patients) of intravenous iron in heart failure with iron deficiency reported lower rates of the composite of recurrent heart-failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death at 12 months than placebo [9].

Hair follicle cells divide rapidly and rely on iron-containing enzymes such as ribonucleotide reductase. Telogen effluvium, in which more follicles than usual shift into the resting phase and shed, is described as being triggered by physiological stress including crash diets, postpartum changes, chronic illness, anaemia and hypothyroidism, and shedding typically becomes visible two to three months after the trigger [4]. Hair loss or thinning, brittle or grooved nails and pallor are listed among the symptoms of iron deficiency [3]. Iron status is therefore often measured when evaluating diffuse shedding.

Appearance communities discuss iron mainly as one item in a nutrient check alongside vitamin D, zinc and thyroid function. Pale skin and tiredness are among the commonest signs of deficiency, and endurance athletes may lose iron through foot-strike haemolysis, gastrointestinal bleeding or blood in urine, so people who train hard are among those whose levels are checked [3]. Athletes may benefit from supplementation, and one reference advises that doses be based on tested ferritin because supplementation can sometimes be harmful [10]. Hair-specific trial evidence is limited; guidance on correcting deficiency rests largely on clinical consensus and the general iron-deficiency literature.

Iron sits at the centre of the heme groups in haemoglobin, which carries oxygen from the lungs to tissues, and in myoglobin, which stores oxygen in muscle. It is also central to electron transfer through iron-sulfur proteins and cytochromes [11]. Most of the body's iron is recycled: about 20 mg a day is used to make new red blood cells, mostly from recycled iron, while losses through bleeding, sweat and shed skin and gut lining are roughly 1 mg a day for men and 1.5 to 2 mg for menstruating women, and the body has no regulated way to excrete iron [11].

Absorption typically ranges from 5 to 35 percent of intake. Heme iron from animal products is absorbed more efficiently, about 15 to 35 percent, than the non-heme iron in plants and most supplements, about 10 to 20 percent. Vitamin C enhances absorption while calcium, zinc and manganese reduce it [11]. The 25-amino-acid peptide hormone hepcidin, made mainly in the liver, controls iron release into the blood by removing ferroportin, the only known mammalian iron exporter [11][12].

Iron deficiency is the state in which the body lacks enough iron for its needs; without correction it can progress to iron-deficiency anaemia, and the stage without anaemia is called latent iron deficiency [3]. Common symptoms are fatigue, pallor, headache and breathlessness; less common ones include hair thinning, brittle nails, restless legs, pica and reduced immune function [3].

Causes include blood loss (especially heavy menstrual bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding and blood donation), pregnancy, low dietary intake, malabsorption, certain drugs, parasitic infection and chronic inflammation, which lowers available iron through hepcidin [3]. Diagnosis typically uses a complete blood count together with serum ferritin, iron and total iron-binding capacity; because inflammation raises ferritin, a C-reactive protein test helps interpretation [3]. A 2025 JAMA review addresses diagnosis and treatment of iron deficiency in adults [8].

Heme iron from red meat and poultry is absorbed most easily, and non-heme sources include lentils, beans and fortified cereals; oxalates and phytates reduce absorption [3]. Vegetarians and vegans may need higher intake because plant iron is less readily absorbed [10].

Oral iron raises haemoglobin and ferritin in people who are deficient. Comparisons between formulations are an active research area: a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials compared ferrous bisglycinate, an amino-acid chelate, with other iron supplements for effects on haemoglobin and ferritin in adults and children [13], and a randomised trial in pregnancy reported that 25 mg of iron as ferrous bisglycinate was as effective as 50 mg of iron as ferrous sulfate for preventing deficiency and anaemia [14]. A randomised trial in iron-depleted young women found that oral iron supplements raise hepcidin, the hormone that limits iron uptake, and reduce absorption from subsequent doses, which has been cited in discussion of daily versus alternate dosing [15][12].

For anaemia in pregnancy, randomised trials have compared a single-dose intravenous iron approach with oral iron [16][17]. A 2025 meta-analysis examined the optimal dose and duration of oral iron for children and adolescents with iron-deficiency anaemia [18], and another 2025 meta-analysis examined psychiatric and cognitive outcomes of iron in people who are iron deficient but not anaemic, such as menstruating adults [6]. A review of dietary heme iron discusses its efficacy and tolerability [19].
No randomised trial of iron supplementation for hair growth or other cosmetic outcomes was found. The clinical literature concerns iron deficiency and anaemia in general medical settings.

Meta-analyses and trials include: oral ferrous bisglycinate versus other iron preparations [13][14]; oral dose and duration in paediatric anaemia [18]; intravenous versus oral iron in pregnancy [16][17]; intravenous iron in heart failure with iron deficiency [9]; infection risk associated with intravenous iron compared with oral iron or none [20]; the relationship between iron deficiency and thyroid function [5]; cognitive and psychiatric outcomes in non-anaemic iron deficiency [6]; and the effect of iron on the infant gut microbiome in a Bangladeshi randomised trial [21]. An older randomised trial examined oral iron tolerance [22].

Registered trials include studies of ferrous sulfate versus iron amino acid chelate, sucrosomial iron in ulcerative colitis, intravenous versus oral iron in haemodialysis and inflammatory bowel disease, and iron absorption after gastric bypass [23][24][25][26][27].

Oral iron commonly causes gastrointestinal effects such as nausea, constipation, diarrhoea and heartburn; US product labelling describes these as usually mild, notes that taking iron with meals or reducing the dose may lessen them, and states that dark stools are a harmless result of unabsorbed iron [7]. Tolerability has been the motivation for newer formulations such as ferrous bisglycinate, which trials and a meta-analysis have compared with iron salts for gastrointestinal events [13][14]. A randomised study of oral iron tolerance appeared as early as 1974 [22].

Accidental overdose of iron-containing products is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under six, and labels carry a prominent warning to keep products out of children's reach [7]. Excess body iron is toxic through oxidative stress and tissue damage, as seen in haemochromatosis [1]; iron-dependent cell death, termed ferroptosis, is a separate subject of laboratory research [28][29]. A 2021 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined infection risk with intravenous iron versus oral iron or no iron [20]. Because anaemia can have causes other than iron deficiency, product labels note that it requires investigation to determine its cause [7].

Excess iron damages organs mainly through oxidative stress. Hereditary haemochromatosis, most often involving the HFE gene and especially the C282Y variant, lowers hepcidin so that too much iron is absorbed [30]. It is most common in people of Northern European descent: about 1 in 8 in those groups carry the main variant and roughly 0.5 percent have the condition, with men far more often affected than women [30]. Iron deposits mainly in the liver, heart, pancreas, joints and endocrine glands, and darkening or bronzing of the skin is a classic sign; regular blood removal (phlebotomy) is the main treatment [30]. People with hemochromatosis are advised to avoid iron and vitamin C supplements because vitamin C increases iron absorption [30][10].

Iron is a component of haemoglobin, which carries oxygen, and of enzymes involved in cellular respiration and DNA synthesis [1]. Its absorption is regulated by hepcidin, a hormone discussed in a 2023 review of iron in health and disease [12]; oral iron doses raise hepcidin and reduce absorption of subsequent doses [15]. The proposed link to hair is that follicle cells have high iron demand, and low stores may push follicles prematurely into telogen; this is a physiological hypothesis rather than a result established in hair-specific trials.

Elemental iron has atomic number 26 and exists mainly as iron(II) and iron(III) in compounds [2][1]. Supplements use ferrous salts, chelates and polysaccharide complexes with differing tolerability and bioavailability profiles [13].

Oral forms include ferrous sulfate, fumarate, gluconate and succinate; injectable forms include iron dextran, iron sucrose, ferric carboxymaltose and others. Injections are used when oral iron fails, is not tolerated or a fast response is needed, and cost more [10]. Benefits may appear within days, but normalising iron stores can take up to two months or more [10].

Iron can bind other drugs, including tetracyclines, quinolones, levodopa and bisphosphonates, reducing absorption, and calcium, antacids, tea and phytic acid also reduce iron absorption; spacing doses a few hours apart is the usual labelled guidance [10]. Ferrous salts appear on the WHO list of essential medicines and are sold as generics and over the counter [10]. Iron pills have been in use since at least 1681, and Blaud's pills, named after the French physician P. Blaud, were the first widely known form [10].

Iron deficiency is a major global burden; Global Burden of Disease analyses list it among leading causes of years lived with disability [31][32], and an estimated 1.9 billion people worldwide had anaemia as of 2021, according to one summary [1].

In bodybuilding and physique forums, iron appears occasionally in blood-test threads, often alongside advice that markers be checked before supplements are started. Looksmaxxing discussions of hair loss list ferritin among the labs people ask for when shedding is diffuse rather than patterned, since diffuse shedding is the pattern associated with telogen effluvium [4]. A distinct looksmaxxing protocol centred on iron is not documented.
